block1.heading: Galungan marks the triumph of good over evil, and the homecoming of ancestral spirits.
paragraphs: It is held every 210 days, a full year on the Balinese pawukon calendar, and the whole island prepares for days beforehand. Families cook festival dishes together, and tall bamboo poles are raised in front of every home.
Ancestors are believed to return to their family houses during these days, so shrines are cleaned, fresh offerings are laid out and the house temple is filled with prayer.

block2.heading: Look up on Galungan morning: the streets are lined with penjor.
paragraphs: These arching bamboo poles are dressed in woven palm, fruit, flowers and cloth, and they bow over the road like a procession of dancers.
Visitors are welcome to watch quietly. Wear a sash and modest clothing, and ask before taking photographs of anyone at prayer.

block1.heading: Kuningan closes the Galungan season ten days later, with yellow rice and quiet prayer.
paragraphs: On Kuningan the ancestral spirits are thought to leave the family compound, and households make small offerings of yellow rice, which gives the day its name.
Prayers are said before noon, because the spirits are believed to depart by midday.

block2.heading: In some villages the season ends with a very different ritual.
paragraphs: In the village of Munggu, in Badung, young men join long poles into a great cone and march in a ceremony known as mekotek, a tradition said to ward off misfortune.

block1.heading: Nyepi is the Balinese New Year, and the whole island falls silent for a day.
paragraphs: Falling in March or April by the Saka lunar calendar, Nyepi is spent at home in stillness. There is no work, no travel and no open fire, and even the airport closes.
Hotels keep lights low and curtains drawn, and guests stay on the property.

block2.heading: The silence has its own beauty.
paragraphs: With no traffic and little artificial light, the stars appear in numbers rarely seen on the island, and the sea is as still as glass.
The following morning, families visit one another and the island begins its year with a clear head.

block1.heading: Before the New Year, the village carries its temple treasures to the sea to be purified.
paragraphs: A few days before Nyepi, communities walk to the shoreline in long processions, carrying sacred objects, umbrellas and banners, accompanied by gamelan.
At the water's edge priests lead prayers and sprinkle holy water, washing away the impurities of the past year.

block2.heading: On Sanur Beach, you can watch from a respectful distance.
paragraphs: The beach fills with white and gold clothing. Please keep to the edge of the crowd, silence your phone and never step between the worshippers and the sea.

block1.heading: On the evening before Nyepi, neighbourhoods parade giant demon figures through the streets.
paragraphs: Built by local youth groups over several weeks, the figures of bamboo, paper and paint are carried by teams to the sound of drums and cymbals.
Each represents the unwanted forces of the past year; at the end of the evening many are burned so that the island can start afresh.

block2.heading: The parade is loud, joyful and a little frightening.
paragraphs: Crowds gather at crossroads to watch the figures spin to face the four directions. It is best seen from a safe distance, and children are usually delighted.

block1.heading: Each temple celebrates its own anniversary, called piodalan, with several days of ceremony.
paragraphs: Many temples hold their piodalan every 210 days, and the whole community takes part: women carry towering fruit offerings on their heads, and men prepare food and music.
Priests invite the deities down to the shrines, where they are honoured with flowers, incense and holy water.

block2.heading: If you are invited, dress for the occasion.
paragraphs: Wear a sarong, a sash at the waist and a modest top. Sit lower than the priests, never point your feet at a shrine and join in the blessing with quiet respect.
Our front desk can suggest ceremonies that welcome visitors.

block1.heading: Each summer, Denpasar hosts a month of dance, music and craft from every corner of Bali.
paragraphs: The Bali Arts Festival is held in the Taman Werdhi Budaya art centre, usually from mid-June to mid-July. It opens with a grand parade and continues with performances, exhibitions and food stalls.
It is a chance to see rare dances and village orchestras that seldom perform outside their home communities.

block2.heading: A lively evening out, about thirty minutes from the hotel.
paragraphs: Our team can arrange a driver and a schedule of the best performances. Arrive early, take a seat near the front and stay for the closing dance.

block1.heading: In the old village of Tenganan, young men duel with bundles of thorny pandan leaves.
paragraphs: Known as mekare-kare, the ritual forms part of an annual festival of the Bali Aga people in Karangasem, eastern Bali. Pairs of men fight in a ring, shield in one hand and a bundle of spiked leaves in the other.
The scratches are treated afterwards with a herbal paste, and the competitors embrace.

block2.heading: Alongside it, the village swings in giant wooden wheels.
paragraphs: Girls ride the ayunan jantra, a hand-turned wooden Ferris wheel, in a rite connected with the village's harvest and traditions.
It is a long drive from Sanur, so book a guide and expect a full day.

block1.heading: Twice a month, the island turns to the moon: purnama for the full moon and tilem for the new moon.
paragraphs: On these days families bring offerings and attend temple prayers, and many people wear white. The air smells of incense and frangipani.
Purnama is a time of clarity and blessing; tilem is a quieter day of inward reflection.

block2.heading: A full moon over the water is worth staying up for.
paragraphs: Walk the beach path after dinner and you may see families making offerings at the shore. The moonlight on the sea is bright enough to read by.

block1.heading: Everywhere you look in Bali there is a small offering, set down with care.
paragraphs: The daily offering, called canang sari, is a small palm-leaf tray of flowers, a little rice, a pinch of salt and incense. It is placed on shrines, doorsteps and at crossroads each morning.
Larger offerings, built of fruit and rice cakes, are made for festivals and family ceremonies.

block2.heading: Please step around them, and treat them with care.
paragraphs: The offerings are gifts to the gods and protective spirits, and the ones on the ground are left to the elements. Walk around rather than over them, and never touch the incense or the flowers.
